## Title

**`cleanplots` --** Graphics scheme that implements best data visualization practices. Colors are color-blind friendly and remain distinguishable when printed in black and white, with coordinated marker symbols and line patterns so that groups stay distinct across multiple visual channels.

## Overview

`cleanplots` changes the default look and feel of Stata graphics. The choices of colors, markers, line patterns, gridlines, legend placement, and other aspects of the figure follow best data visualization practices, with no per-graph effort needed.

The color palette is designed for accessibility. It contains no red-green pair (red-green color blindness is the most common form, affecting roughly 8% of men), and the first five colors pass simulation checks for all three major forms of color blindness. The palette also alternates darker and lighter colors so that the first several groups remain distinguishable by lightness alone when a figure is printed in black and white.

Color alone reliably distinguishes about 4-5 groups. Beyond that, addiitonal markers or patterns are needed for distinguishability. `cleanplots` automatically varies markers, line patterns, and other features.

Bar charts, area plots, and pie charts automatically use softer versions of the colors. These elements use far more ink than points and lines, so full-strength colors overwhelm; `cleanplots` fades them for a cleaner look while full-strength colors remain on markers, lines, and outlines.

The default `cleanplots` colors are a nominal palette, meaning no ordering is implied by the colors or markers. When an ordered (ordinal) palette is needed, use the `cleanplots#` schemes on a single graph (see [Ordinal color schemes](help.html#ordinal) below).

For more information and to see examples, see the [cleanplots website here](https://www.trentonmize.com/software/cleanplots).

Many of the features of cleanplots are adapted from the excellent black and white colorscheme plotplain.

## Using cleanplots

To change your graphics scheme to `cleanplots` for all graphs:

```stata
set scheme cleanplots, perm
```

Or apply it to a single graph with the `scheme()` option:

```stata
sysuse auto, clear
graph twoway scatter price weight, scheme(cleanplots)
```

Stata's default graphic scheme is `s2color`. To change back to the default:

```stata
set scheme s2color, perm
```

## The colors

The ten main colors, used for markers, lines, and confidence intervals (shown as the Stata color definition and the resulting hex code):

| # | Definition | Hex | RGB |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | red*1.2 | #D50000 | 213 0 0 |
| 2 | eltblue*.9 | #8FC6EB | 143 198 235 |
| 3 | black | #000000 | 0 0 0 |
| 4 | gs9 | #909090 | 144 144 144 |
| 5 | purple*1.1 | #740074 | 116 0 116 |
| 6 | pink*.3 | #FFB3D9 | 255 179 217 |
| 7 | navy*1.3 | #143755 | 20 55 85 |
| 8 | gs12 | #C0C0C0 | 192 192 192 |
| 9 | gs4 | #404040 | 64 64 64 |
| 10 | lavender*.35 | #D9D7F0 | 217 215 240 |

Bars, areas, and pies use softer versions of the same colors (e.g., eltblue*.7, purple*.9), rendered with 70% intensity. You can verify any of the colors interactively at [Coloring for Colorblindness](https://davidmathlogic.com/colorblind/#%23D50000-%238FC6EB-%23000000-%23909090-%23740074-%23FFB3D9-%23143755-%23C0C0C0-%23404040-%23D9D7F0).

<span id="ordinal"></span>

## Ordinal color schemes

The default `cleanplots` colors are nominal, with no implied ordering:

```stata
sysuse auto, clear
graph bar price, over(rep78) asyvars scheme(cleanplots)
```

To have the colors reflect ordering, use the `cleanplots#` schemes on a single graph. Five are available -- `cleanplots3`, `cleanplots5`, `cleanplots7`, `cleanplots9`, and `cleanplots11` -- where the number is how many sequential colors the scheme provides. Colors run from light yellow to dark navy, so higher categories are darker. For example, for a chart with 5 ordered groups:

```stata
sysuse auto, clear
graph bar price, over(rep78) asyvars scheme(cleanplots5)
```

The ordinal colors are from the cividis palette (Nunez, Anderton, & Renslow 2018), a variant of viridis (van der Walt & Smith 2015) optimized so that readers with red-green color blindness see essentially the same palette as everyone else. Because the colors run monotonically from light to dark, the ordering itself also survives black and white printing.

The `cleanplots#` schemes inherit all layout, sizing, and legend settings from the main `cleanplots` scheme, and each series gets a distinct line pattern and marker symbol for maximum distinguishability. If a graph has more groups than the scheme has colors, the colors recycle (e.g., under `cleanplots3` the 4th group repeats color 1) while the line patterns and marker symbols continue to vary, so recycled groups never share both color and pattern/symbol.

## Updates

`cleanplots` was overhauled in July 2026 to ensure all 10 colors and the choices of lines, markers, etc. are color-blind friendly and work as well as possible in black and white. In addiiton, the ordinal `cleanplots#` schemes were added. Finally, the legend was moved to be at the direct right of the graph

I recommend using the updated scheme. But if you are feeling nostalgic, the older version is preserved as `cleanplots_classic`.

## cleanplots for R

A companion `cleanplots` package for R (ggplot2) shares this scheme's colors, marker symbols, line patterns, and layout. See the full documentation and details on downloading the R package at [tdmize.github.io/cleanplots](https://tdmize.github.io/cleanplots/).

## Authorship

`cleanplots` is written by Trenton D Mize (Departments of Sociology & Statistics [by courtesy] & The Methodology Center at Purdue University). Questions can be sent to tmize@purdue.edu

## Citation & References

In general, I do not think the use of a graphics scheme requires citation. So for most cases, feel free to use cleanplots without citation. But, if you need/want a citation you can cite cleanplots as:

Mize, Trenton D. 2017. "cleanplots: Stata graphics scheme for easy and effective data visualizations." https://www.trentonmize.com/software/cleanplots

If using the ordinal `cleanplots#` schemes, please also credit the cividis colors:

Nunez, Jamie R., Christopher R. Anderton, and Ryan S. Renslow. 2018. "Optimizing colormaps with consideration for color vision deficiency to enable accurate interpretation of scientific data." PLOS ONE 13(7): e0199239.
